title: Detecting drift before an upgrade
summary: How a diff shows changes made outside Helm.

steps.n: Before applying, the engineer asks what would change.
The plugin loads the manifest of the stored release.
It also reads the objects as they are in the cluster.
The new chart and values are rendered.
The output shows a replica count that someone edited by hand, plus the planned changes.
The engineer decides whether to keep or overwrite the manual change and records it in version control.

title: A system call, step by step
summary: How a program asks the kernel to read a file.

steps.n: The program calls a library function and does not touch the hardware itself.
The library puts the call number in a register and executes an instruction that switches the CPU to kernel mode.
The kernel finds the open file from the descriptor and checks that reading is allowed.
If the page cache does not hold the data, the kernel asks the disk for it.
The block is placed in the page cache and the process is woken.
The kernel copies the data to the program buffer and switches back to user mode. strace shows this exchange.

title: How the OOM killer acts
summary: What happens when memory runs out.

steps.n: The application touches new pages and the kernel needs physical memory for them.
The kernel first reclaims cache and swaps out cold pages.
If reclaim fails, allocation cannot succeed.
The kernel scores processes by memory use and their oom_score_adj.
The chosen process is killed immediately and cannot clean up.
dmesg shows the killed process, its memory use and a table of candidates.

title: A write and fsync
summary: Why a write can return before data is on disk.

steps.n: The application writes and the kernel copies the data into a page of the cache.
The call returns quickly while the page is marked dirty.
The application asks that its data reach stable storage.
The dirty pages are handed to the flusher.
The device receives the data and flushes its own cache.
Only now is the data safe against power loss. This is why databases are limited by disk latency.

title: From power on to login
summary: The main stages of a Linux boot.

steps.n: The firmware tests hardware and chooses a boot entry.
GRUB or a similar loader starts from the boot partition.
The bootloader loads the kernel with its command line and a small temporary root filesystem.
The kernel loads drivers, assembles storage and mounts the real root filesystem.
The kernel starts systemd as the first process.
systemd starts services in dependency order until the login prompt or network services are ready.

title: A full connection tracking table
summary: Why new connections fail while CPU is idle.

steps.n: A client opens a connection through the gateway.
The kernel needs a table entry to track and translate the flow.
The table already holds nf_conntrack_max entries.
The kernel drops the packet and logs a message.
The client sees timeouts although the application servers are idle.
The operator raises the limit with memory in mind and shortens timeouts.

title: Changing a kernel setting for good
summary: Runtime change versus persistent change.

steps.n: The engineer changes the value on the running system.
The new limit applies immediately to new listeners.
On reboot, the change is not remembered.
The kernel boots with its built-in default and the problem comes back.
The engineer saves the setting in a file under /etc/sysctl.d.
Reloading applies it now and the file applies it at every boot.

title: How a pipeline runs
summary: Processes connected by pipes.

steps.n: The shell splits the command line at pipe characters.
The shell starts each command as a process and connects standard output to the next input.
All commands run at the same time, linked by pipes.
Data flows from grep into sort as it is produced.
sort needs all input before it can output, then uniq counts duplicates.
The pipeline returns the status of the last command unless pipefail is set.

title: A request with retry and backoff
summary: How a script survives a flaky API.

steps.n: The script sets a timeout so it never waits forever.
The client sends the request over the network with the timeout set.
The API reports a temporary problem.
The client waits before trying again, with random jitter.
The second attempt is sent after the pause to give the API time to recover.
The result is returned. After a few failures the client stops and raises a clear error.

title: Keep-alive connections
summary: Why reusing a connection saves time.

steps.n: A new connection needs a TCP handshake and a TLS handshake before data.
The first request is sent over the new connection.
The server keeps the connection open.
The client keeps the connection in a pool.
The next request skips the handshakes and starts at once.
Unused connections are closed by timeouts. Middleboxes may close them earlier.

title: Failing over with a health check
summary: How a load balancer stops sending to a broken server.

steps.n: A client sends a request to the load balancer address.
The balancer picks a healthy server.
Server A stops answering the check path.
After several failures the balancer removes A from rotation.
New requests keep arriving while server A is still broken.
Traffic goes to the remaining healthy server until A passes checks again.

title: What docker run does
summary: From image to running process.

steps.n: The CLI sends the request to the daemon.
If the image is not local, the daemon downloads the layers.
Layers are stacked read-only with a writable layer on top.
The kernel isolates processes, network and mounts and applies resource limits.
The image command becomes process 1 in the container.
Traffic to host port 8080 reaches port 80 in the container.

title: A canary release
summary: Sending a small share of traffic to the new version.

steps.n: The pipeline starts the new version beside the old one.
The router sends a small share of traffic to the canary.
Metrics from the canary are compared with the stable version.
If the canary meets the targets, the pipeline continues.
Traffic is shifted in steps with checks between them.
If error rates rise, traffic returns to the stable version at once.

title: A rolling update
summary: How a Deployment replaces pods without downtime.

steps.n: The engineer changes the image in the Deployment.
The controller adds a pod with the new template, within maxSurge.
The new pod receives traffic only after its readiness probe succeeds.
An old pod is stopped, within maxUnavailable.
The controller continues in small steps until all pods are new.
kubectl rollout status reports success. A failing probe stops the rollout and keeps old pods.

title: Why a pod is in CrashLoopBackOff
summary: How restarts slow down after repeated failure.

steps.n: The kubelet starts the container.
The application stops because of bad configuration.
The kubelet restarts it after a short delay.
The same error repeats on every start because nothing has changed.
The delay grows up to five minutes and the pod status shows the back-off.
The engineer reads the last run logs and describe events to find the cause.

title: Plan and apply
summary: How Terraform compares code, state and reality.

steps.n: The engineer asks what would change.
Terraform loads what it believes exists.
It queries the cloud for the current settings.
The plan lists additions, changes and destroys for review.
After approval, Terraform makes the calls.
The state is written with the new resource IDs.

title: Assuming a role
summary: How a service gets temporary credentials.

steps.n: The service asks to assume a role.
The trust policy says who may assume the role.
The check passes because the caller identity is on the trust list.
The service receives credentials that expire soon.
The service calls the resource with them.
The permission policy of the role limits what succeeds. No long-term keys are stored.

title: One request traced across services
summary: How a trace connects spans.

steps.n: The user request reaches the gateway, which creates a trace ID.
The ID travels in a header to the next service.
The orders service starts a span for its database query.
The query takes 900 ms, far longer than the other steps.
The span ends and the response returns.
In the trace view, the long database span is clearly the cause.

title: Spending an error budget
summary: How an SLO guides release decisions.

steps.n: The team agrees on a target for successful requests.
The remaining allowance is the error budget for the period.
An outage uses most of the budget.
With little budget left, the team focuses on reliability work.
Work is prioritised on the causes of the outage.
When the period resets or the budget is healthy, normal releases continue.

title: Rotating a leaked secret
summary: The order of actions after a secret leaks.

steps.n: The first step makes the leaked value useless.
A new value is generated in the secret manager.
Services fetch the new secret at the next refresh or restart.
The responder looks for use of the old secret from unknown addresses.
Copies in repositories and tickets are removed.
Scanning, shorter lifetimes and review of the cause close the incident.

title: A playbook run
summary: How Ansible changes servers over SSH.

steps.n: The control node reads the playbook and selects hosts from the inventory.
The inventory returns the matching hosts and variables.
Ansible connects and collects information about each server.
Each task is a module with a desired state, run on every host.
A changed file notifies a handler.
The handler restarts the service once. A second run reports no changes, which shows idempotence.

title: Replication and lag
summary: Why a read replica may return old data.

steps.n: The application writes to the primary.
The primary records the change in its log.
The replica receives and applies the changes.
A read on the replica comes before the change is applied.
The application sees stale data. This delay is called replication lag.
Read-your-writes cases use the primary or wait for the replica.

title: Cherry-pick a fix
summary: Copying one commit to another branch.

steps.n: The fix is committed and reviewed on main first.
The developer switches to the release branch.
Git creates a new commit with the same change on top of the branch.
If the surrounding code differs, the developer edits and continues.
The release change is reviewed like any other.
After checks pass, the fix is merged and a patch release is tagged.

title: How text becomes tokens
summary: What the model reads and what you are billed for.

steps.n: Your application sends the prompt as ordinary text.
The tokenizer cuts the text into small pieces, roughly four characters of English each.
Each token becomes an ID number that the model can process.
The model reads all token IDs together and builds context from them.
Input and output tokens are counted for the request.
The response includes token counts, which you log to track cost and limits.

title: The next-token loop
summary: How one answer is produced one token at a time.

steps.n: The model receives all prompt tokens as its starting context.
It computes a probability for every possible next token.
The sampler chooses a token based on the probabilities and the temperature setting.
The chosen token is added to the output.
The new token becomes part of the context for the next step.
The loop ends at an end token or the length limit, and the stop reason is reported.

title: Filling the context window
summary: Why long chats and big documents run into a limit.

steps.n: The system prompt is sent first on every request and always uses space.
Each turn adds the question and the answer, so the history gets longer.
Retrieved text or files are added and may take thousands of tokens.
Room for the answer must remain, because input and output share the window.
If the total is too large the request fails or older parts must be removed.
Your application removes or summarises old turns so the important parts still fit.

title: What temperature changes
summary: How the same prompt can give different answers.

steps.n: The model gives each candidate token a probability, such as 60, 25 and 15 percent.
A low temperature makes the likely token even more likely.
Answers are nearly the same each run, which suits extraction and classification.
A high temperature gives unlikely tokens a better chance.
Answers differ between runs, which suits brainstorming but is harder to test.
Even at low temperature you check required properties over several runs, not exact text.

title: Why the API forgets
summary: How a chat works when the API is stateless.

steps.n: The user sends the first message.
Your application sends the system prompt and message one.
The model replies and keeps nothing about the exchange.
Your application saves both messages in its database.
The user sends a follow-up that depends on the first answer.
Your application sends the earlier messages plus the new one, which is why the model seems to remember.

title: Streaming a response
summary: How tokens reach the screen before the answer is finished.

steps.n: The browser asks for an answer and keeps the connection open.
The server calls the API with streaming turned on.
The API sends text pieces as soon as they are produced.
The server passes each piece to the browser, which shows it at once.
A last event carries the stop reason and the usage counts.
Structured data is parsed only when the full reply has arrived and the stop reason is normal.

title: Prompt caching
summary: How a repeated prefix becomes cheaper and faster.

steps.n: The first request puts a long, unchanging manual at the start of the prompt.
The provider stores the processed prefix for a short time.
The first request is billed at the normal input rate plus a small write cost.
The second request begins with exactly the same text.
The stored work is reused, so the answer starts sooner.
The reused tokens are billed at a lower rate, and the usage report shows cache reads.

title: Handling a rate limit
summary: Why retrying at once makes things worse.

steps.n: A batch job sends many requests at once.
The API answers with a rate limit error and may include a retry-after time.
The worker waits for the longer of the retry-after time and a growing delay.
A small random amount is added so workers do not all retry together.
The worker tries again with lower concurrency.
If failures continue, an alert warns the team instead of looping forever.

title: A grounded answer with retrieval
summary: How supplying facts reduces invented answers.

steps.n: A customer asks about the returns policy.
The index returns the few most relevant policy passages.
The passages are placed in tags with the question and a rule to answer only from them.
The model answers and quotes the sentence it used.
The reply links to the source passages so the customer can check.
Known test questions confirm that the right passage is still found after each update.

title: A reply cut off by the limit
summary: Why JSON sometimes fails to parse.

steps.n: The request asks for a large JSON document with a small output limit.
The model writes tokens until the limit is reached.
The reply ends in the middle of a string and the stop reason says max_tokens.
A careless pipeline sends the text straight to the parser.
The parser fails because the JSON is unfinished.
A good pipeline reads the stop reason, raises the limit or shortens the task, and tries again.

title: Prompt, retrieve or fine-tune
summary: How to choose how to give a model what it needs.

steps.n: Clear instructions and examples solve many problems cheaply.
An evaluation set shows whether the prompt is good enough.
If the answer needs private or changing facts, retrieve them at request time.
Check that answers are correct and cite the retrieved text.
Training helps with a stable style or format that prompting cannot achieve.
Compare quality gain with data work and maintenance, and keep the evaluation as the judge.

title: Evaluation in CI
summary: How a model or prompt change is checked before release.

steps.n: A change to a prompt or model version is proposed.
The pipeline loads saved realistic inputs with expected properties.
Each case is sent to the model, several times where variation matters.
Checks in code score format, required facts and forbidden content.
The pass rate is compared with the last release and a minimum.
The pull request fails with the failing cases listed if the rate drops.

title: Investigating a bad answer
summary: How stored traces explain a wrong answer.

steps.n: A user shares the time and the question that went wrong.
The engineer finds the stored prompt, retrieved text, parameters and model version.
The needed fact is missing from the retrieved text.
The index was not updated after the document changed.
The question is added to the evaluation set with the expected fact.
The index job is repaired and an alert watches for stale documents.

title: Parts of a good prompt
summary: What each piece of a prompt is for.

steps.n: One clear sentence says what the model must produce.
Saying who reads the result sets tone and detail.
The text to work on is wrapped in tags so it is not mixed with instructions.
Limits such as length and what to avoid are written as measurable rules.
The exact output shape is described, with an example if needed.
The reviewer checks answers on varied real examples, not one sample.

title: How examples steer output
summary: Why a few good examples beat a long description.

steps.n: Choose three to five realistic inputs that cover normal, borderline and unknown cases.
Each example shows the exact output format and wording wanted.
The examples are added in a consistent layout before the real input.
The model copies the format and the decision style from the examples.
Cases that are not in the prompt measure whether the pattern generalises.
If one label is over-predicted, examples are rebalanced and definitions added.

title: Reasoning before answering
summary: When step-by-step thinking helps and when it costs.

steps.n: The model answers a multi-step question in one go.
The evaluation set shows many mistakes on steps in the middle.
The prompt asks the model to work through the steps before the final answer.
Accuracy rises, but tokens and delay also rise.
The final answer is placed in its own tag so code can extract it.
Simple lookups stay direct, and hard tasks keep the reasoning step.

title: Layout of a system prompt
summary: Where rules, data and user text belong.

steps.n: Stable instructions about role, boundaries and style go first.
The required output format and error behaviour are stated clearly.
Documents are added in tags and marked as data, not instructions.
The actual question comes last, close to where the answer begins.
The model uses the rules, the data and the question together.
Secrets and permission checks stay in code, because prompt text can often be revealed.
